query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal pre‐treatment that promotes the in situ formation of a self-healing, tribo-catalytic oxide/nanolayer on the high-entropy alloy surface will simultaneously lower both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a broad temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated high-entropy alloy components that exhibit high friction and rapid wear under sliding contact, especially when operating from moderate (≈50°C) to high (≈500°C) temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal pre-treatment (annealing in an air environment at optimized temperatures and durations) designed to trigger controlled surface oxidation and formation of a lubricious oxide or nanoflake layer.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear conditions under normal loads across service temperatures from ca. 50°C to 500°C, with the treatment parameters optimized to form the protective layer without inducing detrimental bulk phase changes.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-generated, tribo-catalytic and self-healing oxide/nanolayer (e.g., a dense, continuous composite oxide such as ZrTiO4 or similar lubricious nanolayer) that forms on the alloy surface during thermal pre-treatment and regenerates during service.
generation.mechanism: The thermal pre-treatment initiates controlled surface oxidation that produces a continuous lubricious oxide layer. This layer minimizes direct asperity contact and absorbs shear stresses during sliding, thereby reducing friction while also protecting the substrate from material loss and wear. The self-healing nature of the layer ensures that any local damage is rapidly mitigated by further oxidation when exposed to the environmental oxygen during service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the pre-treated alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly reduced coefficient of friction and lower wear rate, with these improvements maintained consistently over a wide service-temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy currently shows high friction and wear rates due to insufficient intrinsic lubrication and surface protection under variable thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only when the thermal pre-treatment parameters (temperature, time, and atmosphere) are carefully controlled to form a stable and ductile oxide/nanolayer without compromising the bulk mechanical properties; performance outside the tested temperature range (50°C to 500°C) or under extreme loading conditions not covered in the experiment remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: While the available evidence supports the beneficial role of a controlled oxide layer in reducing friction and wear, the exact optimal treatment window and the long-term stability of the self-healing nanolayer under cyclic loading remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. Subject one set to the controlled thermal pre-treatment under the optimized conditions and use the other set as the untreated control. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding wear tests across a range of temperatures from 50°C to 500°C under controlled normal load and sliding speed conditions. Assess the surface post-testing for layer continuity and regeneration.
measurements: Wear rate measured via mass loss or profilometry
Surface morphology and oxide/nanolayer characterization using SEM, EDS, and XRD/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal pre-treated samples do not consistently exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the untreated controls across the full range of tested temperatures, or if the lubricious oxide/nanolayer fails to form or maintain its integrity during sliding tests, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.

frame.system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) components used in self‐lubricating moving parts in their as‐fabricated (untreated) state, which currently exhibit high friction and wear rates under service conditions.
frame.goal: Achieve a significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a broad temperature range (e.g., from moderate to high temperatures) without compromising the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
frame.limitation: The untreated HEA presently shows excessive friction and wear, particularly under varying thermal conditions, limiting its effectiveness in demanding tribological applications.
constraints: A single intervention must address both friction and wear simultaneously
The improvement must be robust across a wide range of temperatures (e.g., from approximately 50°C to 500°C)
The intervention should not adversely affect the bulk mechanical properties and other functionalities of the HEA
regime: Wide temperature spans that mimic service conditions (moderate to high temperatures)
prior_attempts: Incorporation of secondary phases that did not consistently reduce both friction and wear across all temperatures
Surface coatings and multilayer deposition methods that improved one property at the expense of the other or degraded thermal stability
Techniques borrowed from steels or ceramics (e.g., added lubricious phases) but not optimized for the unique microstructural complexity of HEAs

decision.trend: Early work on HEAs for wear resistance focused on modifying alloy composition (e.g., adding W or tailoring dual-phase BCC structures) and processing routes (e.g., spark plasma sintering, laser cladding) to improve hardness and high‐temperature performance. However, these approaches frequently resulted in trade‐offs between friction reduction and wear resistance or produced benefits only over a limited temperature regime. More recent studies, such as those exploring 2D HEA nanoflakes with tribo‐catalytic activity and amorphous HEA films that form protective oxide layers upon thermal shock, have shifted focus toward surface/interface engineering. These methods aim to create a self‐generated, lubricious surface film that can adapt to temperature changes, yet a robust intervention that simultaneously lowers both friction and wear across a broad temperature range still remains unachieved.
decision.unsolved: A single, integrated intervention that reliably reduces both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range—without degrading the bulk mechanical properties of the HEA—remains elusive. In particular, ensuring that a self-lubricating surface modification can form and regenerate in situ under both moderate and high temperatures is still an open challenge.
decision.lever: Controlled in situ formation of a tribo-catalytic, self-healing oxide/nanolayer (such as through a targeted thermal pre-treatment that triggers the formation of a lubricious 2D HEA nanoflake layer on the surface)
decision.why: This approach logically extends recent trends where surface-engineered layers have been shown to dramatically lower friction and wear by activating tribocatalytic or self-lubricating mechanisms. By preconditioning or depositing a nanoscale layer that forms a protective, lubricious oxide under service conditions, the treatment can address both friction and wear simultaneously across a wide temperature span while preserving the core mechanical integrity of the untreated HEA.
